title: GIAC GCIA
summary: GIAC GCIA (Global Information Assurance Certification Certified Intrusion Analyst) is an advanced, vendor-neutral certification for analysts who detect and characterise intrusions from network and host telemetry. It is aimed at senior security operations analysts, network security engineers, threat hunters and forensic practitioners who already read packets and logs fluently and want to prove they can reconstruct activity from raw evidence rather than from a vendor console summary. Passing the exam shows an employer that the holder can interpret packet captures, flow records, intrusion detection alerts and system logs, distinguish ordinary protocol behaviour from manipulation, and describe an intrusion precisely enough that another analyst can verify the conclusion independently. The exam is proctored and open-book with multiple-choice and multiple-answer items and a scaled passing score, and the questions are heavily evidence driven: a short capture excerpt or log fragment is presented and the candidate must state what happened, which protocol or mechanism was in use, or what should be examined next. Hands-on practice is what separates candidates. Building genuine familiarity with packet analysis, writing and tuning detection signatures, correlating flow data against host logs, and working through captures with known ground truth develops the pattern recognition the exam rewards, while candidates who only read about analysis tend to lose time re-deriving protocol fundamentals under the clock. GCIA is regarded as one of the more demanding defensive certifications because it requires evidence-level fluency, not vocabulary.
objectives: Network traffic analysis fundamentals: Read packet captures at the protocol level and distinguish normal behaviour from anomalies in the protocols most commonly abused.
TCP and IP behaviour: Explain connection state, fragmentation, tunnelling and encapsulation well enough to recognise traffic that has been deliberately manipulated.
Application layer protocols: Interpret domain name resolution, web, mail, file transfer and remote access exchanges, and identify how each is used for legitimate or hostile purposes.
Intrusion detection and signature engineering: Interpret, write and tune detection signatures while accounting for false positives, evasion techniques and performance limits.
Traffic baselining and anomaly detection: Establish what normal looks like for a given network, then reason about deviations without over-trusting statistical outliers.
Flow and metadata analysis: Use flow records and similar metadata to scope activity, identify regular beaconing and reconstruct connections at a scale packet capture cannot reach.
Host and log correlation: Combine system, application and security logs with network evidence to confirm an intrusion rather than infer one from a single source.
Attack patterns in evidence: Recognise reconnaissance, tunnelling, command and control, and exfiltration patterns from the artefacts each leaves behind.
Analyst reporting and escalation: Document findings, confidence levels and next investigative steps so that a peer can reproduce the conclusion.
